When you say something aside, you are stepping away — even if just for a moment — from the main conversation, story, or topic, to say something that is separate from it. Think of it like opening a small side door during a conversation, stepping through it to say something quick, and then stepping back in and continuing as before.

That is what an aside is: a remark or comment that is set apart from the main flow of what is being said or written.

The word "aside" as a noun is used in two main situations: one in theatre, and one in everyday speech and writing. Both share the same core idea, but with a small and interesting difference.

1. The Theatrical Aside

In a play or dramatic performance, an aside is when a character on stage says something directly to the audience — words that the other characters on stage are not supposed to hear.

Imagine two characters, Alice and Bob, are having a conversation on stage. Suddenly, Alice turns toward the audience, lowers her voice slightly, and says: "He has no idea I already know his secret." Then she turns back to Bob and continues talking normally. That little moment — that private comment to the audience — is an aside.

It is a storytelling tool. It lets the audience peek into a character's true thoughts, feelings, or intentions, even while the scene keeps moving forward. The other characters on stage act as if it was never said.

Key features of the theatrical aside:

  • It is spoken out loud, but only the audience is meant to "receive" it.
  • It is brief — a sentence or two, not a long speech.
  • It pauses the main action for just a moment, then lets it continue.
  • It reveals something hidden — an inner thought, a secret, a private reaction.

2. The Everyday Aside

Outside of theatre, an aside is a comment or remark that is not directly part of the main topic being discussed. It is a brief detour — something you say or write that is related, interesting, or worth mentioning, but is not the central point.

For example, imagine someone is explaining how to bake a cake. They say: "Mix the flour, eggs, and sugar together. As an aside, this same recipe was used by my grandmother for forty years. Anyway, once the batter is ready, pour it into the pan."

That middle sentence — the one about the grandmother — is an aside. It is not part of the instructions. It is a small, supplementary comment. Then the speaker returns to the main topic.

You will very commonly see the phrase "as an aside" used to signal that what follows is one of these detour-comments. It is a polite, clear way of telling the listener: "This isn't the main point, but I want to mention it briefly."

Key features of the everyday aside:

  • It is secondary — not the main message.
  • It is brief by nature. A long digression would simply be a digression, not an aside.
  • It is often relevant to the broader topic, just not the immediate point.
  • It can appear in both speech and writing.

Both uses of "aside" share one essential quality: separation from the main flow. In theatre, the aside is separated from the other characters. In conversation, it is separated from the main topic. In both cases, it is a small, contained, secondary moment — a brief step sideways before returning to the main path.

• "In the final act, the villain delivers a chilling aside to the audience, revealing he planned the murder from the very beginning." → theatrical use
  • "The professor mentioned, as an aside, that Einstein had failed his university entrance exam — before going back to explaining the theory of relativity." → everyday use
  • "Her aside to the crowd drew more laughter than anything else in the play." → theatrical use
  • "I should mention, as an aside, that I am not a doctor — please verify this with a professional." → everyday use

It is worth noting that an aside is not an interruption. An interruption breaks the flow and takes over. An aside is gentler — it briefly steps outside the main conversation with full awareness that it is doing so, and then steps back in. It knows its place. It does not try to become the main event.

That self-awareness — that quality of being deliberately secondary — is really the heart of what makes something an aside.
